desc:
A binary string is alternating when no two adjacent characters are equal, such as "0101" or "10101". In one operation you may flip any single character ('0' becomes '1' and vice versa).

Return the minimum number of flips needed to turn s into an alternating string.

For example, s = "0100" needs 1 flip (change the last character to get 0101), s = "10" needs 0, and s = "1111" needs 2.
constraints: s contains only the characters '0' and '1'
hints: How many different alternating strings of length n exist?
Exactly two: one starting with '0' (0101...) and one starting with '1' (1010...). The result must be one of them.
The number of flips to reach a target is the number of positions where s differs from it. Count the mismatches with 0101...; the mismatches with 1010... are then n minus that. Return the smaller.
editorial: An alternating string is fully determined by its first character, so there are only two candidates of length n. Each flip fixes at most one position, and every mismatching position has to be flipped, so the cost of reaching a candidate is exactly the Hamming distance to it.

Count m = the number of indices i where s[i] differs from i % 2 (the pattern 0101...). Every position differs from exactly one of the two patterns, so the distance to the other pattern is n - m. The answer is min(m, n - m), computed in O(n) time and O(1) space.
